opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in this whole space. When people see results from systems where an LLM proposes code changes, you evaluate them, and you keep the good ones in an archive, there's a tendency to read it as the model inventing things from scratch. In practice the starting solution does a lot of work in defining what's even reachable.

There are a few ways it shapes things. First, it sets the representation. If you seed the system with a particular program structure, say a specific way of packing circles or a training loop written a certain way, the LLM will mostly make local edits around that scaffold. It's very good at mutating, refactoring, and recombining, but it tends to stay in the basin you put it in. So a strong starting point often gets you fast, solid improvements, but it can also anchor you and limit how far you can drift.

Second, there's a real trade-off between a good seed and a minimal one. If you start from something very simple, almost a blank program, you sometimes see more diverse and surprising solutions, because the model isn't committed to anyone's design choices. But you pay for it in compute and in many early generations that don't evaluate at all. If you start from a near-state-of-the-art solution, you're mostly doing refinement, and it gets harder to say whether anything is new or just a well-tuned version of what a human already wrote.

That's why I think the evaluation of these systems needs to be more honest about the seed. When someone reports a new result, I want to know: what did you start from, how much prior knowledge was baked into the initial program and the prompt, and how sensitive is the outcome to that choice? Ideally you'd run from several different seeds, including deliberately weak ones, and see whether the system converges to similar ideas or finds genuinely different ones.

And this connects to the open-endedness question more broadly. Real discovery seems to require escaping your initial framing, not just optimizing within it. So things like maintaining diversity in the archive, novelty pressure, letting the system propose new sub-problems or rewrite the scaffold itself, I think those matter as much as the strength of the base model. The starting solution is a prior, and the interesting research question is how to build systems that can use that prior without being trapped by it.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong starting point can anchor the system in its existing basin and limit how far it drifts, conveying the local-optima constraint.

r002.rationale: It says a very simple or nearly blank starting program can produce more diverse and surprising solutions.

r003.rationale: It mentions higher compute costs and early generations that may not evaluate, but does not clearly state that finding a good solution may require a long search.

r004.rationale: It says a strong starting point can yield fast improvements, but does not clearly connect inductive biases in the starting solution to more efficient convergence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated aspects of these systems. People tend to focus on the search procedure, the prompting strategy, how you structure the evolutionary loop, but the starting point does an enormous amount of work in determining where you end up.

So the way I think about it is that the initial solution essentially defines the basin you're searching in. When you give an LLM a seed program, say a baseline implementation of some algorithm, the model is going to propose edits that are local in a particular sense. Not local in the way gradient descent is local, but local in terms of the conceptual neighborhood of what it has been shown. It reads the code, it forms a kind of implicit model of what this thing is trying to do, and then its proposals are variations on that theme. So if your seed is a very conventional solution, you tend to get polished, incrementally improved conventional solutions.

And that's actually fine for a lot of use cases. If what you want is a well-tuned implementation of a known idea, starting from a strong baseline is great, you converge fast. But if you want genuine novelty, something that would surprise a domain expert, a strong starting point can actually be a trap. The model anchors on it. Every mutation inherits the architecture and the assumptions baked into the seed, and the system spends its compute budget refining rather than exploring.

What we found interesting, and this came up quite a bit in the work on things like the AI Scientist and also with the discovery-oriented experiments, is that sometimes a deliberately weak or minimal seed produces more diverse trajectories. If you start from something almost skeletal, a stub that satisfies the interface but doesn't commit to much, the model has to fill in the blanks, and different lineages in the population will fill them in differently. You get much more structural diversity early on, and then selection can act on that diversity. Whereas with a strong seed, your population at generation ten often looks like ten slightly different versions of the same program.

There's a related point about what the LLM has seen during pretraining. If the seed solution is something that's extremely common on the internet, a textbook implementation, the model has very strong priors pulling it back toward that canonical form. You'll propose a weird edit, and three generations later the model has quietly reverted it because the canonical version is a stronger attractor. So in a way, the starting solution and the prior interact. A seed that's in distribution is sticky. A seed that's a bit off-distribution gives the model less to anchor on, which can be liberating but also riskier because you lose the stability.

I'd also say the starting solution shapes what the system even thinks the problem is. The seed carries implicit framing, how the inputs are represented, what the decomposition is, what's treated as fixed versus variable. Those framing choices propagate. One of the things I'm most interested in right now is whether you can get these systems to question the framing itself, to say, actually, this whole representation is wrong, let me reformulate. That's where the big discoveries historically come from in science, and it's precisely the thing a seed solution tends to suppress, because the seed has already made those decisions for you.

So practically, I think the honest answer is that there's a trade-off between convergence speed and exploration, and the seed is one of your main levers for it. If I want reliability, I start strong. If I want surprise, I start minimal, run multiple independent populations with different seeds, and I'm much more tolerant of early generations that look bad on the metric, because that's often where the structural novelty is incubating. And ideally you'd have the system itself learn to manage that, to recognize when it's stuck polishing and deliberately restart from a different formulation. We're not fully there yet, but I think that meta-level control over where you begin is going to matter at least as much as the search operators themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says a strong seed can trap the system in its architecture and assumptions, causing it to spend its budget refining rather than exploring; it describes the seed as defining the search basin.

r002.rationale: It says a weak or minimal seed produces more diverse trajectories and structural diversity because the model has room to fill in the blanks in different ways.

r003.rationale: The response notes that minimal seeds can yield bad early generations and be riskier, but does not state that an unconstrained start may require a long search to find a good solution.

r004.rationale: It explains that a strong seed carries assumptions and framing that constrain later proposals, and says a strong baseline helps the system converge quickly on a known idea.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting solution has a huge influence, because it gives the model a frame for what the solution is supposed to look like. If you give it a very polished implementation, it can be quite good at making local improvements, but it may also inherit all the assumptions baked into that implementation. So you can get better performance without really exploring a different approach.

Starting from something simple, or even deliberately weak, leaves more room for exploration. But then you’re asking the system to discover the basic structure as well, and that can consume a lot of your search budget. There’s a trade-off between giving it a useful foothold and anchoring it too strongly.

What I’d want to do is vary the starting points. Give it several structurally different solutions, perhaps include an almost empty one, and see whether the searches converge. And the evaluation matters enormously: if you can reliably test a candidate, you can keep a surprising idea because it works, even if it looks nothing like the initial solution. That’s where you have a chance of moving beyond just polishing what you supplied.

r001.rationale: The response says a polished implementation may anchor the search and limit exploration, but it does not clearly state that a highly optimized start can leave the system stuck in local optima.

r002.rationale: It says a simple or deliberately weak start leaves more room for exploration and recommends structurally different starting points.

r003.rationale: It says a simple or weak start makes the system discover basic structure, which can consume a lot of search budget.

r004.rationale: It mentions a useful foothold and a trade-off, but does not state that inductive biases in the starting solution can make optimization converge more efficiently.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting solution matters enormously, because it gives the model a frame for what the solution space looks like. If you start with a very strong, highly engineered implementation, the model tends to make local changes: tune a constant, replace a component, rearrange something. That can be productive, but you may also be anchoring the search to assumptions that are difficult to escape.

If you start from something simpler, there’s more room for structural changes. The tradeoff is that you might spend a lot of your budget rediscovering things you already knew. So I wouldn’t say that a weaker starting point necessarily produces more novelty. It’s really an interaction between the initialization, the feedback you provide, and how you maintain diversity in the search.

What I find interesting is running from different starting points and asking whether they converge to the same kind of solution. If they do, perhaps the objective is pushing you quite strongly in that direction. If they don’t, then your initialization is effectively determining which regions of the space you get to explore. And that’s a reason to treat the starting solution as part of the experimental design, rather than just a convenient piece of code to get the system running.

r001.rationale: It says a highly engineered start tends to produce local changes and can anchor the search to assumptions that are difficult to escape, conveying the risk of getting trapped in local optima.

r002.rationale: It says a simpler start leaves room for structural changes, but does not clearly state that it enables exploration of diverse solutions.

r003.rationale: It says a simpler start may spend budget rediscovering known results, but does not state that an unconstrained start may require a long search to find a good solution.

r004.rationale: It discusses initialization affecting which regions are explored, but does not state that constraining inductive biases make optimization converge more efficiently.
